title: The Sound of Harlem
objective: Students will analyze the musical structures of Harlem Renaissance jazz and blues — call-and-response, the 12-bar blues form, improvisation, syncopation, and the role of the rhythm section. They will connect these structures to their African musical roots and understand how jazz was simultaneously a new American art form and a continuation of African musical traditions. Students will respond through structured listening, notation analysis, or original composition.
materials: Audio clips — ideally one each of: 12-bar blues (Bessie Smith), jazz improvisation (Louis Armstrong), big band (Duke Ellington), and stride piano (Fats Waller). All available free via Smithsonian Folkways or YouTube
Optional: piano or keyboard for demonstrating the 12-bar blues chord progression live
Differentiated handouts — one per student; pencils for notation work
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** Bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit. **Option 2 — Virtual visit:**

steps.title: Listen and compare
script: Play 30 seconds of straight classical music, then 30 seconds of Louis Armstrong. No introduction.

*“Same instruments — woodwinds, brass, strings in the classical piece, brass in the jazz. But they sound completely different. In the next 30 seconds, write down three things that make the jazz sound different from the classical piece. Be specific — not just ‘it’s more fun.’”*
Take responses. Students will typically identify: rhythm (swung/syncopated vs straight), improvisation, call-and-response, the feel of the beat, expression. Affirm and build on these.

screen.question: What makes jazz sound like jazz?

steps.purpose: Hear the difference first; name it after.
students: In the next 30 seconds, write down three things that make the jazz sound different from the classical piece. Be specific — not just ‘it’s more fun.’

steps.title: Call-and-response
script: Build the structural vocabulary in layers:

**Call-and-response:** Rooted in West African music and work songs — one voice calls, another answers. In jazz, the trumpet “calls,” the rhythm section “responds.” Play an example, ask students to identify it.
steps.purpose: Hear call-and-response, and where it comes from.
students: Listen: which instrument calls? Which responds?

steps.title: Syncopation
script: **Syncopation:** Emphasis on the off-beat — the “and” between the beats rather than the beat itself. The defining rhythmic feel of jazz and blues. Clap a regular beat, then clap the syncopated version.

screen.text: Emphasis on the off-beat — the “and” between the beats rather than the beat itself.

steps.purpose: Feel the off-beat in the body before naming it.

steps.title: 12-bar blues form
script: **12-bar blues form:** The harmonic foundation of most early jazz. Play or demonstrate the I–IV–I–V–I progression. Point out: the same 12 bars repeating gives musicians a framework to improvise within.
steps.purpose: See the framework that gives musicians something to improvise within.
students: The same 12 bars repeat. What does that let musicians do?

steps.title: Structure and freedom
script: **Improvisation:** Creating melody spontaneously within the harmonic structure. Not random — constrained by key, chord changes, and musical conversation with other players.

*“Louis Armstrong wasn’t just playing notes — he was having a conversation with the other musicians in real time. The structure gave him the rules; improvisation gave him the freedom. That combination — structure and freedom — is the defining idea of jazz.”*

screen.text: The structure gave him the rules; improvisation gave him the freedom.

steps.purpose: Put the pieces together: the defining idea of jazz.
students: Where do you hear the structure? Where do you hear the freedom?

steps.title: Choose a handout

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Guided listening response to one jazz recording — identify instruments, describe mood, mark where they hear call-and-response, and answer five structured questions. No notation required.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Listen to two contrasting recordings (blues and big band jazz). Complete a comparison framework covering structure, instrumentation, improvisation, and emotional effect. Write a paragraph connecting jazz structure to African musical roots.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Full structural analysis of one jazz recording: identify 12-bar form, mark syncopation, annotate call-and-response, and evaluate the improvisation. Composition task: write an original 4-bar melodic phrase over a provided blues chord progression, with written rationale for note choices.

steps.purpose: Listen, analyze or compose at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.
